title: A piecewise or kink curve: where does it switch regime?
summary: A curve built from different rules on different intervals. Shaded bands name each regime and marked breakpoints show exactly where the rule changes, so a corner is read as a change of law and not as a plotting glitch.

media.alt: A teal curve made of a quadratic piece, a rising straight line and a falling straight line, with three shaded regime bands, two orange dashed breakpoints at x = -1.5 and x = 1, and a note that the slope jumps at both.
media.caption: Reference render of class F1.4 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: Where does it switch regime?
read_the_figure.axes: x: the independent variable, -3 to 3.5. y: f(x), -1.3 to 3.6. Vertical dashed lines mark the breakpoints; the shaded bands and the text at the bottom name the regimes.
look_at: Where are the breakpoints, and what is f there? (x = -1.5 with f = -0.5; x = 1 with f = 2.5.)
Is f continuous at each breakpoint? The two pieces meet at the same height, so there is no jump in f.
What happens to the slope at each breakpoint? It jumps: a corner.
Which regime is steepest, and does any regime have a slope of the opposite sign?
as_drawn: Three regimes: a quadratic on the left (flat at its end), a line of slope 1.2 in the middle, a line of slope -0.4 on the right.
Both breakpoints are drawn as amber diamonds on dashed vertical lines, with a coordinate label and a leader line.
The note at the top right says f is continuous but f' jumps at both breakpoints. That is exactly what the picture should let you check.
read_the_figure.proves: That the function changes rule at the marked points and is continuous there. It does not prove that the rule inside a band is what its label says: only the formulas and data can do that.
if_wrong: No breakpoint marks: a corner looks like an accident of resolution.
A jump discontinuity drawn as a joined line: the curve appears continuous when it is not.
Few samples near a breakpoint: the kink is rounded and the breakpoint location is misreported.

terms.meaning: A value of x where the formula that defines f changes.
An interval on which one formula holds; also a physical mode of behaviour (elastic, plastic).
No jump in f at a point: the left and right limits agree with the value.
A point where f is continuous but the slope jumps. The derivative does not exist there.
The change of f' across a breakpoint, right slope minus left slope.

remember: Mark every breakpoint on the axis, with its x value.
Continuous does not mean smooth: check f and f' separately.
A jump discontinuity needs a gap or open and closed dots, not a joined line.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: A line mark carries the function. Vertical dashed lines and diamond markers carry the breakpoints. Background bands carry the regime, with a short text label. The note carries the continuity statement in words.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: The question is about a change in the law, not about a shape. Marking the breakpoints on the axis and naming each interval turns an anonymous bend into an explanation: this part is quadratic, this part is a straight line with slope 1.2. The eye can check continuity (the pieces meet) and the slope change (the angle at the corner).

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Joining sample points by a line hides jumps. A coarse sample rounds off a corner and shifts the apparent breakpoint. Shaded bands can suggest a region is more important than it is. And a smooth-looking join can still hide a jump in the derivative that matters for physics (a sudden change of stiffness).

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: Marked breakpoints let a reader quote where the switch happens. Without them the reader must estimate it from the corner, and the estimate is poor for a gentle change of slope.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Plot f' underneath (F1.2) to see the jumps as steps. Use open and closed circles for a jump discontinuity. If the regimes are power laws, a log-log view (F1.6) makes each a straight line with its own slope.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a second panel with f' as a step function and print the slope jump at each breakpoint. Draw the tangent lines of neighbouring regimes extended through the corner.

steps.title: Continuity at a breakpoint
steps.note: At x_b = -1.5: quadratic 0.2(x + 1.5)^2 - 0.5 gives -0.5, line -0.5 + 1.2(x + 1.5) gives -0.5. At x_b = 1: -0.5 + 1.2 x 2.5 = 2.5 and the right line 2.5 - 0.4(x - 1) = 2.5. Both agree.

steps.title: The slope jump
steps.note: At -1.5: slope 0 (bottom of the parabola) to 1.2, a jump of +1.2. At 1: from 1.2 to -0.4, a jump of -1.6. The second corner is a peak of f in this window.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) where are the breakpoints and what is f there? (2) What are the slopes in the regimes? (3) Is f continuous?

solution.text: Breakpoints at x = -1.5 and x = 1, with f = -0.5 and f = 2.5 read from the diamonds.
Regime II slope = rise over run between the diamonds, from -0.5 to 2.5 over 2.5 units; regime III slope is read from the end, 2.5 at x = 1 to 1.5 at x = 3.5.
The pieces meet at each diamond with no vertical gap, so f is continuous; only f' jumps, by +1.2 and -1.6.

worked.answer: Breakpoints -1.5 and 1; slopes 1.2 and -0.4; f is continuous and not differentiable at the two corners.

analyze.q: A material's stress-strain curve is a piecewise function. What would the breakpoints and regimes be, physically?
If f' were drawn beneath, what would it look like at each breakpoint?
Why does a corner at a peak matter for finding the maximum with calculus?

evaluate.q: A design rule is written as a smooth formula fitted through a piecewise curve. When is that acceptable and when dangerous?
evaluate.hint: Compare the error near the breakpoints with the quantity you care about.

create: Make a piecewise curve with a jump discontinuity and draw it correctly with open and closed dots.
Plot f and f' together, and label the slope jump values at each breakpoint.

checks.q: What distinguishes a corner from a jump on a plot?
checks.hint: Look at the heights on either side.
checks.answer: At a corner f is the same on both sides and only the slope changes. At a jump f itself differs on the two sides.

checks.q: A regime has slope 1.2 and is followed by a regime with slope -0.4. What is the slope jump?
A line plot of 10 points shows a smooth bend where theory says there is a sharp corner. What happened?
checks.hint: How many points are near the breakpoint?
checks.answer: The coarse sampling and the line join rounded the corner. Sample densely near the breakpoint or plot the pieces separately.
